name: ScaleSee
headline: Make a large number feel like a real difference.
summary: A visual comparison tool that turns quantities into scenes while keeping the meaning of scale explicit.
role: Visual explanation, comparison journeys & interaction design
problem: A ratio can be mathematically clear and still be difficult to picture. ScaleSee turns two quantities into a shared visual comparison, choosing a representation that fits the kind of quantity instead of using the same chart for everything.
process: I selected a visual reference appropriate to each kind of quantity: a ground line for height, nesting for land, or a shared course for speed. The reference is part of the explanation.

An extreme ratio creates a useful design tension: showing true scale can make one quantity nearly disappear. A compressed alternative needs an explicit label that remains with a shared comparison or exported image.

decisions.title: Choose the picture to fit the quantity
decisions.choice: Height shares a ground line, land can be nested, and speed uses a common course.
decisions.reason: A meaningful reference can make a ratio easier to interpret than a generic bar.
decisions.tradeoff: Every visual metaphor introduces assumptions; those assumptions need to be stated where they affect the comparison.

decisions.title: Keep scale transformations explicit
decisions.choice: True scale and logarithmic scale are separate modes.
decisions.reason: When a small quantity almost disappears, that can be the honest answer; a compressed alternative should declare the change.
decisions.tradeoff: A log view can make a scene more legible while reducing intuitive proportionality.

decisions.title: Let the comparison leave the tool
decisions.choice: A URL carries the selected comparison and an image export preserves the current drawing.
decisions.reason: An explanation is more useful when someone can bring it into the conversation that prompted it.
decisions.tradeoff: An exported image needs labels and scale context because it no longer has interactive controls beside it.

outcome: The tool offers quantity-specific comparisons, explicit scale modes, sharing, and image export. My design focus makes a numerical relationship inspectable and portable. Correct interpretation of extreme ratios remains a question for user evaluation.
reflection: The design lesson is that legibility and proportional truth sometimes pull in different directions. The interface should help the reader understand which trade-off a view makes.
nextSteps: Proposed study: ask readers to estimate the ratio before and after each view, including an extreme comparison and a logarithmic one.
Proposed check: confirm labels, units, assumptions, and scale mode survive in every shared or exported artifact.

name: Where Would I Be…?
headline: Give deep time one personal point of reference.
summary: An interactive globe that lets a chosen place move with a plate-motion model and makes the model’s limits part of the story.
role: Experience framing, interaction sequence & spatial explanation
problem: Plate motion is slow enough to be invisible in everyday life and large enough to reshape a world over time. This project gives that scale a personal anchor: choose a place, move the clock, and follow the ground beneath it.
process: I gave the opening one task: choose a place. A time control and a short result then introduce motion, with optional detail kept out of the main globe.
The visual story needs to carry its qualification with it. Constant-motion extrapolation can invite exploration, but the result should not read as a reconstruction or prediction of the continents.

decisions.title: Give each stage one main task
decisions.choice: Choose a place first, then explore time, with optional comparison later.
decisions.reason: A clear sequence can make a complex subject approachable without presenting every control at once.
decisions.tradeoff: Progressive disclosure should not hide the model’s most important qualification until after someone has formed a false impression.

decisions.title: Protect the space where the answer is drawn
decisions.choice: The design keeps the main globe clear and groups controls in a bottom dock.
decisions.reason: The selected point and its path are the explanation; a floating panel over them would compete with the result.
decisions.tradeoff: A dock must adapt to available height so it does not consume the same space on a small screen.

decisions.title: Make the scientific boundary legible
decisions.choice: The source describes plate movement as a constant-motion extrapolation with increasing limits over long horizons.
decisions.reason: Personal storytelling can encourage exploration without claiming to know the future shape of continents.
decisions.tradeoff: A smooth animation can still imply certainty, so the qualification belongs near the time result.

outcome: The globe connects location selection, time exploration, optional layers, and comparison. My UX direction gives deep time a personal entry point while keeping the model boundary near the result. Understanding that distinction still needs evaluation.
reflection: The interaction succeeds as a question someone can explore, not as a forecast. I would test whether the person leaves understanding both plate motion and why the long-term path is conditional.
nextSteps: Proposed study: ask a visitor to describe what changed and what assumptions the model makes after a short exploration.
Proposed checks: narrow-screen globe visibility, reduced-motion behaviour, keyboard interaction, and whether uncertainty stays visible at extreme dates.

name: The Blog
headline: Make publishing feel like writing.
summary: An editorial site with a browser-based publishing workflow for poems, essays, fiction, and serial writing.
role: Editorial structure, reading experience & author workflow
problem: A personal writing practice should not require a technical deployment ritual for every post. The Blog connects a reading experience with a browser editor that handles content, images, drafts, and publishing through a familiar form.
process: I framed writing, reviewing, and publishing as separate commitments. The editor should support the author’s work without requiring technical knowledge of how a post reaches the website.

The reading experience follows the form of the writing: poetry keeps its line breaks, while topics and series help a reader continue. Publication feedback should make draft and live states easy to distinguish.

decisions.title: Give publishing a clear state
decisions.choice: Draft and published are separate states, with a deliberate release action.
decisions.reason: Writing and releasing a piece are different commitments and should remain distinguishable.
decisions.tradeoff: Publishing can take time. The author needs clear confirmation of what is saved and what is live.

decisions.title: Let the content form affect the layout
decisions.choice: Poetry preserves line breaks and an appropriate verse treatment, while ordinary articles retain a reading layout.
decisions.reason: The way a piece is written can be part of its meaning.
decisions.tradeoff: Formatting conventions must be discoverable in the editor rather than depend on hidden technical knowledge.

decisions.title: Make ongoing writing navigable
decisions.choice: Topics and series connect related pieces within the editorial structure.
decisions.reason: A reader should be able to follow a thread without knowing the order it was published.
decisions.tradeoff: The documented title-based series matching is convenient but implicit; a visible series field would make mistakes easier to avoid.

outcome: The site connects a reading experience with an editorial publishing path. The UX contribution makes room for poems, essays, series, drafts, and release feedback, so the author can focus on the writing and the reader can follow it.
reflection: The important shift is from making content fit the tool to making the tool respect the writing. I would next make publishing status and series membership more visible to the author.
nextSteps: Proposed evaluation: publish a draft, update an existing post, and add a series instalment without using development tools.
Proposed measure: accidental publication, broken links after slug edits, and clarity about whether the latest save is live.

name: The Office Games
headline: Make the next person’s turn obvious.
summary: A team-trivia experience exploring quick room entry, visible roles, and shared game state for a short social break.
role: Social game concept, room journey & turn-taking UX
problem: A short team game loses momentum when people are unsure how to join or whose turn it is. The reviewed Office Games module centres on a simple room flow, a lobby, team roles, and a visible answering/stealing sequence.
process: I mapped the reviewed trivia journey from joining a room to understanding teams, turns, answering, and stealing. The broader games catalogue is outside the evidence available for this case study.
The UX needs to explain the connection mode before a group commits to a game. Trying a local demonstration and joining colleagues on separate devices are different experiences.

decisions.title: Make joining a small action
decisions.choice: A four-letter room code and a player name provide a concise entry path.
decisions.reason: A social break should spend more of its time playing than explaining setup.
decisions.tradeoff: A short code still needs clear invalid-room and full-room handling, and does not establish secure identity.

decisions.title: Expose responsibility in the game state
decisions.choice: The interface distinguishes answering and stealing teams, active players, and scores.
decisions.reason: People need to see who can act and why the round is waiting.
decisions.tradeoff: Role-based interaction becomes confusing if waiting states or connection loss are not explained.

decisions.title: Keep connection mode understandable
decisions.choice: The setup distinguishes a local demonstration from connected play.
decisions.reason: A demo can help someone try the game, but should not promise multi-device play it cannot provide.
decisions.tradeoff: A connected game needs clear waiting, conflict, reconnection, and host-recovery states.

outcome: The reviewed trivia module connects joining, teams, round state, scoring, and chat. My UX focus makes the social sequence and responsibility for the next action visible. Local demonstration and connected play need distinct expectations.
reflection: The design opportunity is a shared understanding of what happens next. I would assess joining, waiting, and recovery as carefully as the answer-selection screen.
nextSteps: Proposed study: run a short trivia session with several participants and record setup explanations, confused turns, and waiting time.
Proposed checks: separate-device joining, reconnection, duplicate actions, host departure, and a clearly labelled local demo mode.

name: Forma
headline: Give every health reading its context.
summary: A native Android health app that brings activity, sleep and personal trends together while making sources, missing data and experimental estimates visible.
role: Product concept, health-data journeys & interaction design
status: Native Android app · experimental wellness estimates
problem: A watch can collect more measurements than a person can comfortably interpret. A number also changes meaning when it is old, incomplete, imported or estimated. I framed Forma around a daily overview that stays useful without making uncertain data look more reliable than it is.
process: I organised the experience around five destinations: Today for a daily overview, Sleep for the recorded night, Move for activity and workouts, Trends for comparison, and Health for the measurement library. The native app is the product; the React version in the repository is a design preview.

The data constraints shaped the UX. Samsung Health must share records through Health Connect, permissions can be partial, and not every watch measurement is available. Connection setup therefore needs to explain availability rather than treat an empty reading as a failure or a zero.

The later function audit separated Devices from Your data, moved optional personal tools into settings, removed controls without a working purpose, and put formulas behind expandable details. The archived screens illustrate the native visual direction; the audit and current source establish the later navigation and scope. This is an artifact-based retrospective, without a participant study or clinical validation.

decisions.title: Distinguish recorded, missing and estimated values
decisions.choice: Keep source labels and measurement times attached to readings. Preserve gaps in histories, identify sample data, and distinguish sleeping heart rate from a recorded resting-heart-rate value.
decisions.reason: A recent refresh does not mean a sensor reading is recent. People need to understand what a value represents before comparing it with yesterday or using it to interpret their day.
decisions.tradeoff: These labels add density. The hierarchy has to keep essential provenance visible while leaving longer explanations available on demand.

decisions.title: Let a score open into its explanation
decisions.choice: Show the score and its contributing values first, then offer the calculation and diagnostics in an expandable sheet. Recovery requires recorded sleep and a usable baseline vital; missing inputs can leave the estimate unavailable.
decisions.reason: An unexplained score can look authoritative. Showing its inputs makes the estimate inspectable and lets the interface explain why the same score can accompany different activity records.
decisions.tradeoff: Transparency does not validate the model. Sleep, recovery and body-energy estimates remain experimental wellness interpretations, distinct from Samsung proprietary scores and medical assessment.

decisions.title: Separate connecting a device from managing data
decisions.choice: Devices leads with connection state and the next available action. Your data contains coverage, export, optional import and local reset. Targets and personal tools have their own settings paths.
decisions.reason: Someone trying to connect a watch should not have to interpret a coverage report or navigate file-management controls before granting access.
decisions.tradeoff: Separating the tasks adds destinations. Clear names and back paths matter, particularly when permissions are partial or a watch has not synced.

outcome: Forma offers a native daily overview, dedicated sleep and movement views, inspectable histories and a searchable health library. The UX contribution is a hierarchy that connects an overview to the evidence behind it. The repository documents native and emulator checks; physical Samsung sharing remains device-dependent, and the score models are not clinically validated.
reflection: The most useful simplification was giving each kind of detail a clear home. Connection help belongs with Devices; coverage belongs with Your data; a calculation belongs behind its score. I would next check whether people can explain an unavailable or older reading as confidently as a complete one.
nextSteps: Proposed study: ask people to distinguish sample, shared, direct-watch, older and unavailable readings, then explain what an experimental recovery score does and does not mean.
Proposed device checks: follow granted, denied and partial-permission journeys on a Samsung phone and watch, including delayed sync, expired direct readings and corrected history.
Proposed measures: connection-task completion, mistaken interpretations of missing data, and success finding a score explanation or exporting records.

name: OhCaptain
headline: Make the next fleet decision clear.
summary: A 3-v-3 naval game exploring shared command, role-specific decisions and a combat interface that keeps the sea in view.
role: Game concept, captain/operator journeys & tactical interface design

facts.label: captain and two operators per crew

problem: In OhCaptain, sailing and firing are only part of the job. Each crew shares supplies, but its captain decides how to spend them. Operators need to request help while both roles keep track of a changing battle. I framed the interface around the next decision a player can actually make.
process: I separated the crew journey into choosing a station, entering solo play or assembling a room, deploying, and managing the battle. A captain still sails and fights; the extra responsibility is distributing shared supplies. Operators request upgrades or repairs rather than spending the treasury themselves.

The documented Clear Deck revision gives combat a compact score/clock, fleet-alive counts, hull status and a persistent map. Spending moves into the Fleet drawer, while the expanded overview holds rosters, recent events and relay details. Warnings compete for a small number of attention slots instead of becoming a wall of banners.

I reviewed the local playable build, documentation and awareness rules. Solo play with AI fill and peer-to-peer rooms are distinct product paths. Online scope depends on a host keeping the page open; the prototype has no dedicated match service or host migration. Rule checks and seeded scenarios do not establish balance or usability with human crews.

decisions.title: Make responsibility visible before deployment
decisions.choice: Offer Captain and Vessel Operator as distinct stations. Captains distribute shared supplies through the Fleet drawer; operators use the same crew context to request an upgrade or repair.
decisions.reason: A shared resource needs a clear decision owner. Role-specific actions let people understand why they can request something but cannot buy it directly.
decisions.tradeoff: The captain can become a bottleneck while also sailing and fighting. Pending requests need to remain discoverable without forcing a panel over combat.

decisions.title: Keep essential battle state on the field
decisions.choice: Keep the score, clock, relay balance, fleet-alive counts, hull and corner map available. Put spending in a drawer and detailed rosters, events and defenses in the expanded overview.
decisions.reason: The map helps connect local action to the relay objective. Separating routine awareness from deliberate inspection leaves room to aim and navigate.
decisions.tradeoff: An overview can interrupt action. Solo overview pauses the match; online play continues, so players need to understand that distinction. The prototype targets keyboard and mouse rather than claiming a touch-control experience.

decisions.title: Give urgent feedback a limited attention budget
decisions.choice: Show at most one off-screen enemy bearing and reserve one text cue for critical hull, safe healing or an endangered home relay. Limit outgoing damage feedback to two numbers and keep routine radio outside combat.
decisions.reason: An alert is useful only if it helps a player choose an action. A priority order makes a received hit or low hull easier to notice among effects, ships and objectives.
decisions.tradeoff: A quieter interface can hide context that an experienced player wants. The map and overview must provide a dependable route to that detail, and the priority policy needs human playtesting.

outcome: The prototype connects role selection, solo AI-filled matches, room-based crew play and a single capture-and-hold arena. Its combat interface separates immediate awareness, spending and tactical inspection. The portfolio captures show the actual local game, rather than presenting the cinematic menu artwork as gameplay. Multi-device reliability, competitive balance and player comprehension remain evaluation work.
reflection: A fleet game needs coordination as much as combat. The clearest direction was to make responsibility explicit and reduce the number of things demanding attention at once. I would judge the next iteration by whether a new crew understands who can act, what is urgent and why control of a relay matters.
nextSteps: Proposed playtest: form two crews and ask players to explain their role, request or buy a repair, and identify the relay that matters next without coaching.
Proposed checks: invitation and room entry, role reassignment, a guest disconnecting, restrictive peer-to-peer networks, and an honest explanation when a host leaves.
Proposed observations: missed requests, map-to-world confusion, unnoticed critical alerts and time spent in the overview. Compare these before changing the attention policy.
